extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of mathematics; mathematical problem-solvers and instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and heuristics for discovering, presenting, and teaching mathematical proofs and problem solutions, including use of indirect methods, decomposition, equation setup, signs of progress, and plausible reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish uses of reductio ad absurdum
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between two uses of the “reductio ad absurdum” (and indirect proof): as a tool of research (discovery) and as a means of exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As exposition, long reductio proofs can be painful and tedious for readers (constant emphasis on the initial assumption, repeated words like 'hypothetically', 'supposedly'). As a tool of discovery, reductio can be valuable and may present itself naturally when other means are exhausted. After using reductio for discovery, try to convert or compress it for exposition (rearrange, extract the positive independent argument, or compress into a few striking sentences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Always reexamine proofs for alternative (direct) derivations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a result is derived by reductio or indirect proof, look back at the solution and ask: Can you derive the result differently?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience often shows that indirect proofs can be converted into direct proofs or rearranged so the reductio disappears. Examples: carving out independent positive parts of a reductio (digit-sum/ divisibility by 9 example) or converting Euclid's indirect proof of infinitely many primes into a direct constructive procedure (Q = product+1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overreliance on routine problems
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'routine problem' is one solvable by substituting data into a previously solved general problem or by following a well-worn, step-by-step example with no originality required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine problems may be necessary for practice but making students do only routine problems is inexcusable: it trains mechanical performance without judgment or invention (worse than cookbook exercises). Teachers should provide non-routine opportunities to develop judgment and inventiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of discovery (heuristic humility)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no infallible rules of discovery; heuristics aim to collect typically useful procedures rather than magic solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First rule: have brains and good luck. Second: sit tight and wait till you get a bright idea. Instead of unfailing rules, compile and practice stereotyped questions, suggestions, and mental moves that are typically useful in solving problems (the book presents such a collection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of style (communication)
rubrics_metrics.description: First rule of style: have something to say. Second: if you have two things to say, control yourself—say one, then the other, not both at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this to exposition of proofs and teaching: clarity and orderly presentation matter; avoid overloading the reader/listener with concurrent threads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of teaching (know your subject and a little more)
rubrics_metrics.description: First rule of teaching: know what you are supposed to teach. Second rule: know a little more than what you are supposed to teach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A teacher should have enough mathematics and the right attitude toward problems to impart both knowledge and problem-solving disposition to students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate the various parts of the condition (decompose and recombine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the problem as a whole, then go into detail: consider principal parts—the unknown, the data, and the condition—each by itself; decompose and recombine as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether each part can be written down; decompose into parts fit for mathematical expression. This decomposition is the basis for setting up equations and for choosing useful representations. Beware that a logically unobjectionable decomposition may nevertheless be useless; aim for decompositions 'fit for analytic expression'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting up equations is translation
rubrics_metrics.description: To set up equations means to express in mathematical symbols a condition stated in words—translation from ordinary language into the language of mathematical formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two prerequisites: thoroughly understand the verbal statement and be familiar with mathematical forms of expression. Some verbal idioms cannot be translated word-for-word; you may need to rearrange the condition and keep an eye on the resources of mathematical notation (examples: algebraic problems, geometry with volume/area conditions, analytic geometry symmetry problem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear, expressible signs of progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain mental operations typically useful in solving problems have corresponding clear, expressible signs of progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of clear signs: bringing an additional datum into play (e.g., 'superfluous' chess piece becomes useful), taking into account an essential clause of the condition (formula reflects a restriction), emergence of a simpler analogous problem, visualizing the condition or finding a convenient notation. These signs indicate plausible forward movement; read your list of heuristic operations to recognize such signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect less clearly expressible signs (feelings/inspiration) with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Feelings, moods, and intuitions (e.g., 'it looks good', 'well-balanced plan') are genuine signs of progress though hard to formalize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat inspiration and aesthetic feelings as you treat clear heuristic signs: 'trust, but keep your eyes open'—they can guide effectively but may sometimes mislead. Seek to relate them to underlying mental operations when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use signs to guide action but be aware of their fallibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs of progress help decide whether to continue on a path or try another; their absence warns of blind alleys and their presence bolsters confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs may mislead in individual cases; successful interpretation requires experience. On average signs guide correctly, but persistence and careful reading of signs (and perseverance) can be decisive. Examples: abandoning a path too soon vs. reading a sign another noticed and discovering something important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic syllogism as a pattern of plausible reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristic syllogism: If A then B; B is true; therefore A becomes more credible. This yields a change in credibility (degree), not a demonstrative proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with demonstrative syllogism (If A then B; B false; therefore A false): the heuristic conclusion is vaguer, has magnitude (how much more credible), and rests partly on unexpressed 'invisible' foundations (feelings, unstated reasons). Use heuristic syllogisms to adjust confidence but not to claim demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and role of plausible (heuristic/inductive) reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Plausible reasoning (heuristic/inductive/circumstantial evidence) lacks the certainty of strict demonstration but is indispensable for acquiring new knowledge, especially about the physical world or in invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that plausible reasoning provides indications and guidance rather than proof. Clarify heuristic reasons where possible, but accept that much influential reasoning remains obscure and requires study of probability and related concepts for fuller understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization: test special cases to gain insight
rubrics_metrics.description: Specialization passes from considering a whole class to a smaller set or a single object; testing special cases is often useful for tackling unfamiliar assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a proposed theorem is unfamiliar, examine well-known special cases (e.g., equilateral triangle) to see if the assertion holds and to gain intuition or counterexamples; this can suggest pathways to proof or disproof.
